title: Bending a Gaussian
sub: A 1-D flow from N(0, 1) to two clusters. Every band holds the same probability.

frames.caption: Start with z ~ N(0, 1). The shaded bands each hold exactly 1/12 of the probability. A flow is an invertible map x = g(z); watch what it does to the bands.
Morph a quarter of the way towards the target map. Each point moves, but the bands keep their order: the map is monotone, so it can be inverted.
Halfway. Where the map stretches space (the middle), the bands get wider, and since each still holds 1/12 of the probability, they get shorter. Where it squeezes, bands get narrow and tall.
That is the change-of-variables formula: p<sub>x</sub>(x) = p<sub>z</sub>(z) / |dg/dz|. Density is probability per unit length, so stretching by a factor of 3 divides the height by 3.

The finished flow: a two-cluster distribution, with an exact density at every x and exact samples from g(z). In higher dimensions |dg/dz| becomes |det J|, and the architecture's job is to keep that determinant cheap.
